meta.title: Gulf Pharmacology: Generic Names, SI Units, High-Alert Drugs & Local Formulary
meta.title_en: Gulf Pharmacology: Generic Names, SI Units, High-Alert Drugs & Local Formulary
meta.source_note: Drug name equivalences based on INN (WHO International Nonproprietary Names). SI unit conversions based on IUPAC standards. Gulf formulary notes are general — specific formulary availability varies by facility. Verification recommended.

lay_summary: Gulf nursing licensing exams use generic (INN) drug names and SI laboratory units — not the US trade names and mg/dL values familiar from NCLEX. This module bridges that gap, covering essential drug name equivalences, SI unit conversions, high-alert medication safety, and the key pharmacology knowledge tested across all Gulf Prometric exams.

lessons.title: Generic Drug Names vs US Trade Names: The Gulf Standard

content.intro: All Gulf Prometric nursing exams (SNLE, DHA, HAAD, QCHP, OMSB, NHRA, MOHUAE) use International Nonproprietary Names (INN) — the WHO-approved generic drug names — rather than US trade names. Understanding these equivalences is essential for exam success and safe practice.

sections.heading: Analgesics and Antipyretics
sections.text: Paracetamol (INN) = Tylenol (US brand), Panadol (Gulf brand). Maximum adult dose: 1g every 4–6 hours, max 4g/24 hours (3g in hepatic impairment or alcohol use). Paracetamol is the first-line non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic in Gulf healthcare. Ibuprofen (INN) = Advil / Motrin (US brands), Brufen (Gulf brand common). NSAIDs: monitor renal function, GI risk, avoid in third trimester pregnancy and with known renal impairment. Diclofenac (INN) = Voltaren (brand). Tramadol is a weak opioid agonist used for moderate pain — controlled substance in all GCC states. Morphine sulfate (INN): strong opioid, Schedule I controlled — requires dual-nurse verification.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular and Antihypertensive Drugs
sections.text: Atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol — beta-blockers. Key nursing: do not stop abruptly (rebound hypertension, angina). Hold if HR < 60/min or SBP < 90 mmHg — notify physician. Amlodipine — calcium channel blocker, common for hypertension. Ramipril/lisinopril/enalapril — ACE inhibitors: monitor K+ (hyperkalemia risk), monitor cough (dry cough = ACE inhibitor side effect). Furosemide — loop diuretic: monitor weight, urine output, electrolytes (K+, Na+, Mg2+). Spironolactone — K+-sparing diuretic: monitor hyperkalemia, avoid with ACE inhibitors unless monitored. Digoxin — cardiac glycoside: narrow therapeutic index, monitor for toxicity (bradycardia, nausea, visual disturbances — yellow halos), therapeutic level 0.5–2.0 ng/mL. Atorvastatin/simvastatin/rosuvastatin — statins: take evening dose, monitor LFTs.

sections.heading: Antibiotics, Anticoagulants, and Controlled Drugs
sections.text: Amoxicillin / amoxicillin-clavulanate (co-amoxiclav) = Augmentin brand. Clarithromycin (INN) — macrolide; azithromycin is 5-day course for community infections. Ciprofloxacin (INN) = Cipro (US brand). Metronidazole (INN) = Flagyl brand — anaerobic/protozoal infections, avoid alcohol. Warfarin (INN) = Coumadin (US brand not used in Gulf — warfarin used): monitor INR, narrow therapeutic range. Heparin (unfractionated) and enoxaparin (LMWH) — anticoagulants: dual-nurse check required, monitor anti-Xa levels or aPTT. Methadone and morphine — Schedule I controlled substances in all GCC: dual-nurse verification, witness register, locked storage. Midazolam — benzodiazepine, controlled substance — monitor respiratory depression.

content.clinical_pearl: Gulf exam pharmacology questions use generic names exclusively. If you see 'Tylenol' or 'Coumadin' on an exam, that is incorrect — the exam will say paracetamol and warfarin. More importantly, in clinical practice: always document the generic name. High-alert Gulf drugs that require dual-nurse check: insulin, heparin/enoxaparin, concentrated KCl, morphine, fentanyl, midazolam, chemotherapy.
key_points: Gulf exams use INN generic names — NOT US trade names
Paracetamol (not Tylenol), ibuprofen (not Advil), warfarin (not Coumadin)
Beta-blockers: hold if HR <60 or SBP <90, never stop abruptly
ACE inhibitors: monitor K+ and dry cough
Dual-nurse check: insulin, heparin, concentrated KCl, opioids, chemotherapy

lessons.title: SI Units in Gulf Healthcare: Laboratory Values and Clinical Thresholds

content.intro: Gulf healthcare uses the International System of Units (SI) for all laboratory measurements. Nurses coming from US-trained backgrounds must convert from US conventional units (mg/dL, mEq/L) to SI units (mmol/L, µmol/L). Gulf exam questions present values in SI units.

sections.heading: Glucose: mmol/L (not mg/dL)
sections.text: Conversion: glucose mmol/L × 18 = mg/dL (or divide mg/dL by 18 to get mmol/L). Normal fasting glucose: 3.9–5.6 mmol/L (70–100 mg/dL). Hypoglycaemia: < 3.9 mmol/L (< 70 mg/dL) — mild; < 2.8 mmol/L severe. Hyperglycaemia action threshold in most Gulf protocols: > 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL). DKA: glucose typically > 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) with ketonaemia and acidosis. HHS: glucose typically > 33 mmol/L (600 mg/dL) with osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg. Target glucose in ICU: 6.0–10.0 mmol/L (WHO/IDF guidelines adopted in Gulf).

sections.heading: Electrolytes, Renal, and Haematology
sections.text: Sodium (Na+): normal 136–145 mmol/L (same as mEq/L — unit equivalent for monovalent ions). Potassium (K+): normal 3.5–5.0 mmol/L. Hypokalemia: < 3.5 mmol/L (ECG changes: U waves, flat T). Hyperkalemia: > 5.5 mmol/L (peaked T waves, risk of cardiac arrest > 6.5 mmol/L). Creatinine: normal ~44–97 µmol/L (women) / 62–115 µmol/L (men) — conversion: µmol/L ÷ 88.4 = mg/dL. Urea (not BUN): normal 2.5–7.5 mmol/L (Gulf labs report urea; BUN = urea × 0.467). Haemoglobin: g/dL — normal women 12–16 g/dL, men 13.5–18 g/dL. Haematocrit: % — normal women 36–46%, men 41–53%. Bilirubin: µmol/L — normal total < 21 µmol/L (conversion: µmol/L ÷ 17.1 = mg/dL).

sections.heading: Temperature, Vital Signs, and Paediatric Values
sections.text: Temperature: Celsius (°C) — always. Normal: 36.5–37.5°C. Fever: > 38°C (not 100.4°F). Hyperthermia (heat stroke): > 40°C. Hypothermia: < 35°C. Blood pressure targets in Gulf protocols: systolic < 140 mmHg for most adults; < 130 mmHg for diabetics and CKD per international guidelines. SpO2: % — normal ≥ 95% (≥ 88% acceptable for COPD patients on controlled oxygen). Paediatric normal values: neonatal HR 120–160, infant 100–160, toddler 90–150, school-age 70–120, adolescent 60–100 bpm. Neonatal weight: grams (not pounds) — normal term: 2500–4000g. Respiratory rate: adult normal 12–20/min; tachypnoea > 20/min (NEWS2 threshold: ≥ 25/min = high risk).

content.clinical_pearl: The most common SI conversion tested in Gulf exams is glucose. A question presenting glucose of 2.1 mmol/L is hypoglycaemia (= 38 mg/dL); 33 mmol/L is HHS-range (= 594 mg/dL). For sodium and potassium, mmol/L equals mEq/L numerically — no conversion needed. For creatinine, µmol/L is approximately 88 times larger than mg/dL.
key_points: Glucose in mmol/L: normal 3.9–5.6, hypo < 3.9, DKA > 13.9, HHS > 33
Creatinine in µmol/L: normal 44–115 (divide by 88 to get mg/dL)
Urea (not BUN) in mmol/L: normal 2.5–7.5
Temperature in °C: fever > 38°C, not 100.4°F
Electrolytes mmol/L = mEq/L for Na+, K+, Cl- (monovalent ions)

lessons.title: High-Alert Medications and Controlled Drugs in Gulf Practice

content.intro: High-alert medications carry disproportionate risk of causing significant patient harm when used in error. All Gulf healthcare regulatory bodies mandate specific safety checks for these agents. Understanding high-alert drug protocols is heavily tested across all Gulf Prometric exams.

sections.heading: Insulin: The Highest-Alert Medication
sections.text: Insulin is the single most common cause of medication errors in hospital settings worldwide. Gulf protocols for insulin: independent dual-nurse verification before EVERY administration, correct insulin type (basal vs bolus vs rapid-acting), correct dose in units (U — never write 'U' alone, always 'units' to prevent misread as zero), correct route (subcutaneous or IV per order — never IM), correct timing relative to meals for meal-time insulin. Types: rapid-acting (aspart, lispro, glulisine) — give within 15 min of meal. Short-acting (regular/soluble) — give 30 min before meal. Intermediate (NPH) — once or twice daily. Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec) — no peak, once daily. Premixed (70/30, 50/50) — dual dosing window. Hypoglycaemia risk highest with rapid and regular insulin.

sections.heading: Anticoagulants: Heparin and Warfarin
sections.text: Unfractionated heparin (UFH): dual-nurse verification required. Monitor aPTT (target typically 60–100 seconds = 1.5–2.5× normal). Antidote: protamine sulfate. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH / enoxaparin): weight-based dosing (1 mg/kg SC twice daily or 1.5 mg/kg once daily for treatment). Monitor anti-Xa level in renal impairment. Antidote: partial reversal with protamine. Warfarin: monitor INR — therapeutic range typically 2.0–3.0 (2.5–3.5 for mechanical heart valves). Antidote: vitamin K (slow reversal) or fresh frozen plasma (rapid). Hold warfarin if INR > 3.5 (supratherapeutic) — notify physician. Warfarin interactions: antibiotics ↑ INR, NSAIDs ↑ bleeding risk, St John's Wort ↓ INR.

sections.heading: Concentrated Electrolytes and Other High-Alert Agents
sections.text: Concentrated potassium chloride (KCl): NEVER administer IV bolus — fatal cardiac arrest. Must be diluted before administration. Maximum peripheral infusion rate: 10 mmol/hour (some protocols 20 mmol/hour with ECG monitoring). Central access required for > 20 mmol/hour. Dual-nurse verification mandatory. Concentrated sodium chloride (hypertonic saline 3%): restricted use for severe hyponatraemia under close monitoring — correct Na+ no faster than 8–10 mmol/L per 24 hours (risk of osmotic demyelination). Magnesium sulfate: used for eclampsia and severe asthma — monitor respiratory rate (< 12/min: hold, give calcium gluconate antidote), urine output (< 25 mL/hour: hold), DTRs (absent: hold). Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.

content.clinical_pearl: The key question for any high-alert medication error on a Gulf exam: what is the FIRST action? Answer is always: assess the patient first (are they harmed?), then notify the physician, document accurately, and complete the incident report. For concentrated KCl bolus given IV: assess the patient → call rapid response → notify physician. Never delay assessment to complete paperwork.
key_points: Insulin: dual-nurse check always, write 'units' not 'U', never IM
UFH: monitor aPTT; antidote protamine sulfate
Warfarin: monitor INR 2.0–3.0; antidote vitamin K or FFP
KCl IV: NEVER bolus — dilute always, max 10 mmol/hour peripheral
MgSO4 toxicity: RR <12, absent DTRs — antidote calcium gluconate

lessons.title: Psychotropic Medications, Pain Management, and Ramadan Adjustments

content.intro: Psychiatric medications, opioid pain management, and Ramadan-related medication adjustments are clinically significant areas tested in Gulf nursing exams, particularly relevant to the Gulf healthcare context.

sections.heading: Psychotropic Medications in Gulf Practice
sections.text: Antidepressants: SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram) are first-line for depression and anxiety. Monitor: increased suicidal ideation in first weeks (especially < 25 years), serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, agitation, myoclonus, tachycardia) if combined with MAOIs or other serotonergic drugs — MAOIs require 14-day washout before SSRI. TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine): anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision), cardiotoxic in overdose. Antipsychotics: haloperidol (typical), risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine (atypical). Extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) with typicals: akathisia, dystonia, tardive dyskinesia — treat acute dystonia with benztropine IM. Clozapine: risk of agranulocytosis — mandatory weekly WBC monitoring. Lithium: narrow therapeutic index (0.6–1.2 mmol/L therapeutic), toxic > 1.5 mmol/L — signs: tremor, polyuria, nausea, ataxia, confusion. Monitor renal function (lithium is renally cleared).

sections.heading: Opioid Pain Management
sections.text: Opioids used in Gulf practice: morphine sulfate, fentanyl, tramadol, oxycodone, pethidine (meperidine — used in some Gulf facilities, especially for obstetric pain). All Schedule I controlled substances in GCC: dual-nurse verification, witness register, locked storage, wastage documentation with witness. Assessment before opioid administration: pain score (NRS 0–10 or Wong-Baker FACES for children), respiratory rate (hold if < 12/min), level of consciousness, BP/HR. Opioid overdose reversal: naloxone (Narcan) IV/IM/intranasal — 0.4 mg IV, repeat every 2–3 min, max 10 mg. Duration of naloxone shorter than most opioids — reassess, may need repeat doses or infusion. PCA (patient-controlled analgesia): only the patient presses the PCA button — a family member pressing it bypasses the safety mechanism.

sections.heading: Medication Management During Ramadan
sections.text: During Ramadan, Muslim patients who choose to fast from sunrise to sunset require medication schedule adjustments. Key nursing responsibilities: identify fasting patients on admission, collaborate with the physician and pharmacist to review all medications for Ramadan safety. Medications that cannot be deferred: insulin (adjust type and dose with diabetic team — basal-bolus regimens are safer during Ramadan fasting), antiepileptics (timing adjustment needed, not deferral), immunosuppressants (organ transplant patients — individual consultation). Oral medications: permissible after sunset (Iftar) and before sunrise (Suhoor). IV, IM, inhaler, eye drop medications are debated — most Gulf Islamic scholars consider them permissible during fasting as they are not nutritive. Sublingual and transdermal formulations: generally permissible. Respect the patient's religious choice about fasting — do not pressure to break the fast without medical necessity.

content.clinical_pearl: Ramadan medication management is uniquely tested in Gulf exams. The nurse's role: never unilaterally change a patient's medication schedule for Ramadan — always involve the physician and pharmacist. The correct nursing action when a fasting patient refuses morning medications: document the refusal, notify the physician, facilitate religious accommodation by reviewing whether medications can be safely rescheduled to evening.
key_points: SSRI + MAOI: serotonin syndrome risk — mandatory 14-day washout
Clozapine: weekly WBC monitoring for agranulocytosis
Lithium: therapeutic 0.6–1.2 mmol/L; toxic > 1.5 mmol/L
Opioid reversal: naloxone 0.4 mg IV, repeat 2–3 min interval
Ramadan: involve physician and pharmacist — never unilaterally reschedule

flashcards.question: Generic (INN) name for Salbutamol inhaler brand Ventolin?
Normal fasting blood glucose in SI units (mmol/L)?
DKA diagnosis threshold for blood glucose?
Therapeutic INR range for standard anticoagulation (AF, DVT/PE)?
Therapeutic aPTT range for unfractionated heparin (UFH)?
Maximum safe IV KCl infusion rate (peripheral line)?
flashcards.answer: 10 mmol/hour; NEVER give KCl IV bolus — fatal arrhythmia

flashcards.question: MgSO₄ antidote and when to hold?
flashcards.answer: Antidote: calcium gluconate IV. Hold if: RR <12/min, absent DTRs, urine output <25 mL/hr

flashcards.question: 5 medications requiring independent dual-nurse verification in Gulf?
flashcards.answer: Insulin, heparin, concentrated KCl, opioids, MgSO₄ (and chemotherapy)

mcq_questions.question: A nurse in Dubai (DHA) is preparing to administer pain relief. The physician has prescribed 'paracetamol 1g IV'. The medication label reads 'Perfalgan 1g/100mL'. What is the correct action?

options.A: Refuse to administer — the label name does not match the prescription
options.B: Administer after confirming Perfalgan is a brand name for paracetamol
options.C: Contact the pharmacist to change the prescription to the brand name
options.D: Administer only if the pharmacy rewrites the label

mcq_questions.explanation: Gulf exams use INN (generic) names on prescriptions. Perfalgan is a brand name for paracetamol (the INN). The nurse should verify the generic equivalence and administer after standard two-patient identifier check. Refusing to administer would delay care unnecessarily.

mcq_questions.question: A patient's blood glucose is documented as 15.3 mmol/L. In mg/dL, what does this approximately equal?

options.A: 85 mg/dL
options.B: 153 mg/dL
options.C: 275 mg/dL
options.D: 306 mg/dL

mcq_questions.explanation: To convert mmol/L to mg/dL, multiply by 18. 15.3 × 18 = 275.4 mg/dL ≈ 275 mg/dL. Conversely, divide mg/dL by 18 to get mmol/L. Gulf labs use mmol/L exclusively.

mcq_questions.question: A patient with Type 1 diabetes has a blood glucose of 3.2 mmol/L and is confused. What is this value in mg/dL and what condition does it indicate?

options.A: 57.6 mg/dL — hypoglycaemia
options.B: 32 mg/dL — normal range
options.C: 57.6 mg/dL — hyperglycaemia
options.D: 576 mg/dL — DKA

mcq_questions.explanation: 3.2 mmol/L × 18 = 57.6 mg/dL. Normal fasting glucose is 3.9–5.6 mmol/L (70–100 mg/dL). Below 3.9 mmol/L indicates hypoglycaemia. Confusion is a sign of neuroglycopenia — treat immediately with fast-acting glucose.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer insulin 12 units subcutaneously. Which action is essential BEFORE administration?

options.A: Obtain a second nurse to independently check the insulin type, dose, and expiry
options.B: Ask the patient to verify the dose on the insulin pen
options.C: Document administration before drawing up the dose
options.D: Warm the insulin to body temperature before injection

mcq_questions.explanation: Insulin is a high-alert medication requiring independent dual-nurse verification in all Gulf jurisdictions (DHA, QCHP, NHRA, OMSB, MOHAP, MOH-KW). The second nurse checks: correct insulin type, dose, expiry, and patient identity independently — not together, to avoid confirmation bias. Documentation is done after administration, not before.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is preparing potassium chloride 40 mmol to be added to an IV bag. Which practice is MANDATORY?

options.A: Administer KCl as an IV bolus over 2–3 minutes if the patient is critically low
options.B: Obtain a second nurse to independently verify the KCl before adding to the bag
options.C: Add KCl to the bag in the patient's room at the bedside
options.D: Use a 50 mmol/100 mL concentration for peripheral lines

mcq_questions.explanation: Concentrated KCl is a high-alert medication requiring independent dual-nurse verification before preparation. IV KCl bolus is NEVER given — it causes fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Maximum peripheral infusion rate is 10 mmol/hour. KCl must never be added to bags in patient rooms; it must be prepared in the pharmacy or a designated clean area.

mcq_questions.question: A patient on warfarin therapy has an INR of 4.8. The nurse notifies the physician. Which medication would the nurse anticipate administering?

options.A: Protamine sulfate
options.B: Vitamin K (phytomenadione)
options.C: Calcium gluconate
options.D: Naloxone

mcq_questions.explanation: Vitamin K (phytomenadione) is the antidote for warfarin toxicity. INR >3.0 is supratherapeutic; INR >4.0 carries high bleeding risk. Therapeutic INR for most indications is 2.0–3.0. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin (not warfarin). Calcium gluconate reverses MgSO₄ toxicity. Naloxone reverses opioid overdose.

mcq_questions.question: A patient receiving unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion has an aPTT result of 45 seconds (control 30 seconds). What is the correct interpretation?

options.A: aPTT is therapeutic — continue current dose
options.B: aPTT is supratherapeutic — reduce the infusion rate
options.C: aPTT is subtherapeutic — notify physician to increase the dose
options.D: aPTT is within normal limits — no action needed

mcq_questions.explanation: Therapeutic aPTT for UFH anticoagulation is 60–100 seconds (1.5–2.5× the control value). Control of 30 seconds × 1.5 = 45 seconds (lower therapeutic limit). A result of 45 seconds (1.5× control) is at the subtherapeutic boundary — the physician should be notified. The current value suggests insufficient anticoagulation.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse administering magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) for pre-eclampsia checks the patient and finds: respiratory rate 10 breaths/min, absent patellar reflexes, blood pressure 130/85. What is the PRIORITY action?

options.A: Slow the infusion rate and continue monitoring
options.B: Stop the infusion and administer calcium gluconate IV immediately
options.C: Increase the infusion rate to achieve therapeutic levels
options.D: Reassess in 30 minutes and document findings

mcq_questions.explanation: MgSO₄ toxicity signs: RR <12/min (here: 10), absent DTRs, oliguria <25 mL/hr. RR of 10 and absent patellar reflexes are signs of toxicity — STOP the infusion immediately. The antidote is calcium gluconate 1g IV (10 mL of 10% solution) given slowly. This is a clinical emergency; reassessment in 30 minutes is not appropriate.

mcq_questions.question: A patient with a Ramadan-related question asks the nurse whether he can skip his twice-daily metformin during fasting hours. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Tell the patient it is safe to skip doses during fasting hours
options.B: Tell the patient to take both doses at iftar (breaking fast)
options.C: Advise the patient to consult his physician and pharmacist before changing his medication schedule
options.D: Document the request and inform the patient that medication cannot be adjusted during Ramadan

mcq_questions.explanation: Nurses must NEVER unilaterally adjust medication schedules during Ramadan. The physician (to adjust dose/timing if needed) and pharmacist (for medication-specific guidance on fasting compatibility) must be involved. Metformin schedule during Ramadan is a clinical decision — some patients can take it with the evening meal, others may need a dose reduction. Self-discontinuation risks hyperglycaemia.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse discovers a medication error: a patient received 80 mg of furosemide instead of the prescribed 40 mg. What is the CORRECT sequence of actions?

options.A: Notify the pharmacy → document error → inform physician → complete incident report
options.B: Assess the patient → notify the physician → document in the chart → complete incident report
options.C: Complete incident report → notify physician → document in chart → reassure patient
options.D: Document the error in the chart → alert the charge nurse → do not notify the patient

mcq_questions.explanation: The priority sequence for a medication error is: (1) Assess the patient — is there harm? (2) Notify the treating physician with full details. (3) Document clinical facts in the medical record (what happened, patient status, physician notified). (4) Complete the facility incident report. The incident report is NOT part of the medical record. Never alter documentation after an error.

mcq_questions.question: A patient prescribed a beta-blocker (metoprolol) has a resting heart rate of 52 beats/min and blood pressure of 88/55 mmHg. The next dose is due. What action should the nurse take?

options.A: Administer the dose — bradycardia is an expected effect
options.B: Hold the dose and notify the physician immediately
options.C: Administer half the prescribed dose and reassess in 1 hour
options.D: Administer the dose with extra IV fluids to counteract hypotension

mcq_questions.explanation: Standard Gulf nursing protocol: hold beta-blockers if HR <60 bpm OR systolic BP <90 mmHg, and notify the physician. HR of 52 and SBP of 88 both meet hold criteria. Administering any dose without physician authorisation when hold parameters are met is outside safe practice. Document findings and await physician order.

mcq_questions.question: A patient started on an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) last week reports a persistent dry cough. What is the MOST appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Reassure the patient that this is normal and will resolve in 2–3 days
options.B: Document the symptom and notify the physician — this is a known class effect that may require medication change
options.C: Advise the patient to take the medication at night to reduce cough
options.D: Stop the medication immediately and document in the chart

mcq_questions.explanation: Persistent dry cough is a recognised class effect of ACE inhibitors (due to bradykinin accumulation) occurring in 10–20% of patients. It does NOT resolve spontaneously while the drug continues — the physician must be notified as the medication may need to be changed to an ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker). Nurses cannot stop medication without a physician order.

mcq_questions.question: A patient's serum creatinine is reported as 180 µmol/L. Approximately what is this in mg/dL?

options.A: 0.20 mg/dL
options.B: 1.59 mg/dL
options.C: 2.04 mg/dL
options.D: 20.4 mg/dL

mcq_questions.explanation: To convert creatinine from µmol/L to mg/dL, divide by 88.4. 180 ÷ 88.4 = 2.04 mg/dL. Normal creatinine: approximately 45–90 µmol/L (0.5–1.0 mg/dL) for women; 60–110 µmol/L (0.7–1.2 mg/dL) for men. A value of 180 µmol/L indicates significantly elevated creatinine — assess for acute kidney injury.

mcq_questions.question: A patient taking clozapine (antipsychotic) has been on the medication for 3 weeks. Which monitoring parameter is MANDATORY and why?

options.A: Serum lithium levels — clozapine raises lithium to toxic levels
options.B: Weekly white blood cell (WBC) count — clozapine can cause life-threatening agranulocytosis
options.C: Monthly INR — clozapine increases bleeding risk
options.D: Weekly serum potassium — clozapine causes severe hypokalaemia

mcq_questions.explanation: Clozapine carries a BLACK BOX warning for agranulocytosis (WBC can drop dangerously, leading to fatal infection). WBC must be monitored weekly for the first 6 months, then bi-weekly. If WBC falls below 3.0 × 10⁹/L or absolute neutrophil count below 1.5 × 10⁹/L, clozapine must be stopped immediately. This is a Gulf exam high-yield pharmacology point.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is ordered to write 'insulin 10 U' in the medication administration record. What is the correct documentation practice?

options.A: Write 'insulin 10 U' as abbreviated
options.B: Write 'insulin 10 units' — never abbreviate 'U' as it can be misread as '0'
options.C: Write 'insulin 10 IU' using the IU abbreviation
options.D: Write 'insulin 10U' without a space

mcq_questions.explanation: The abbreviation 'U' for units is on the 'Do Not Use' list in all Gulf jurisdictions — it can be misread as '0', turning '10U' into '100 units', a 10-fold overdose error. Always write out 'units' in full. Similarly, 'IU' (international units) should be written as 'international units'. This is a patient safety standard across DHA, NHRA, QCHP, OMSB, and other Gulf bodies.

mcq_questions.question: Which of the following combinations is MOST dangerous due to risk of serotonin syndrome?

options.A: Metformin + enalapril
options.B: SSRI (sertraline) + MAOI (phenelzine)
options.C: Furosemide + spironolactone
options.D: Atorvastatin + amlodipine

mcq_questions.explanation: Combining an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) with an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor) causes serotonin syndrome — a life-threatening condition with hyperthermia, agitation, muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. An MAOI washout period of 14 days is required before starting an SSRI, and vice versa. This is a high-yield Gulf pharmacology and mental health nursing question.

mcq_questions.question: A patient requires opioid analgesia via a patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump. The patient's daughter asks if she can press the button when her mother is asleep and in pain. What is the CORRECT response?

options.A: Allow the daughter to press the button — family care is encouraged
options.B: Allow the daughter only when the nurse is present to monitor
options.C: Explain that ONLY the patient may press the PCA button — proxy activation is prohibited
options.D: Teach the daughter the correct technique and allow her to use it

mcq_questions.explanation: The fundamental principle of PCA safety is that ONLY the patient presses the button. This prevents over-sedation — a patient who is too sedated to press the button is protected by not receiving additional opioid. Proxy PCA (family or nurse pressing on behalf of the patient) is prohibited in all Gulf jurisdictions and internationally. If the patient cannot self-administer, an alternative analgesic method must be prescribed.

mcq_questions.question: A patient with heart failure requires furosemide 40 mg IV. The nurse notes the patient has a known sulfonamide allergy. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Administer furosemide — loop diuretics do not contain sulfonamide
options.B: Hold the medication and notify the physician — furosemide is a sulfonamide derivative
options.C: Administer half the dose and observe for allergic reaction
options.D: Switch to oral furosemide — allergic reactions only occur with IV route

mcq_questions.explanation: Furosemide (a loop diuretic) contains a sulfonamide moiety and may cross-react in patients with sulfonamide allergy. The nurse must hold the dose and notify the physician before administration. The physician will assess the severity of the sulfonamide allergy and determine whether to proceed, switch to an alternative diuretic (e.g., ethacrynic acid), or pre-medicate. Do not administer without physician authorisation.

mcq_questions.question: A patient's temperature is documented as 38.6°C. What is the correct clinical interpretation?

options.A: Normal body temperature — 38.6°C is within range
options.B: Hypothermia — patient requires warming measures
options.C: Fever — temperature exceeds 38.0°C threshold
options.D: Hyperthermia — life-threatening emergency requiring ice packs immediately

mcq_questions.explanation: In Gulf practice, fever is defined as body temperature ≥38.0°C (100.4°F). Normal oral temperature is 36.1–37.2°C; axillary is 0.5°C lower. A temperature of 38.6°C is fever — notify the physician, obtain blood cultures if ordered, administer antipyretics as prescribed (paracetamol is first-line). Hyperthermia (>40°C / 104°F) is a separate, more severe condition requiring urgent cooling.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is about to administer two medications to the same patient. Which information constitutes the MINIMUM two-patient identifiers required before administration in Gulf hospitals?

options.A: Patient's bed number and room number
options.B: Patient's full name and date of birth (or medical record number)
options.C: Patient's diagnosis and physician name
options.D: Patient's wristband colour and ward name

mcq_questions.explanation: Gulf-wide medication safety standard (DHA, NHRA, QCHP, OMSB, MOHAP, MOH-KW, SCFHS): verify at least two patient identifiers before every medication administration. Accepted identifiers: full name AND date of birth, OR full name AND medical record number. Bed number, room number, and diagnosis are NOT acceptable identifiers — patients can be moved between beds/rooms.
